title: Allopurinol and Alcohol: Can You Drink on Gout Medication?
excerpt: Can you drink on allopurinol? Why alcohol, especially beer, raises uric acid against your gout medicine, which drinks are worst, timing, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on allopurinol? Why alcohol, especially beer, raises uric acid against your gout medicine, which drinks are worst, and warning signs to know.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no dangerous chemical reaction between allopurinol and a drink or two. Alcohol doesn't stop the pill from working the way it blocks some antibiotics or interacts with sedatives. The problem is that alcohol, and beer in particular, pushes your uric acid in the opposite direction. Allopurinol is trying to lower uric acid; drinking raises it and makes your kidneys clear less of it. Drink often or heavily and you can partly cancel out the medicine, and a big night out is one of the classic triggers for a gout flare, even for people on treatment. Most people taking allopurinol can still drink a little. The goal is to drink in a way that doesn't undo what the pill is doing.

**The quick rules:** Keep drinking light and occasional, not daily. Beer is the worst choice for uric acid, spirits are in the middle, and wine appears to be the least problematic in moderation. Never skip your allopurinol dose because you plan to drink, and don't take extra the next day to "make up" for it. Drink plenty of water alongside alcohol. If you've just started allopurinol, be especially careful, because the first few months are when flares are most common. And if you develop a rash of any kind while taking allopurinol, stop drinking, call your doctor the same day, and don't take another dose until you've spoken to them.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your allopurinol and knows your kidney function, other medicines, and gout history. **Talk to your doctor before drinking on allopurinol if** you have kidney disease, liver disease, frequent flares, tophi (chalky lumps under the skin), or kidney stones, or if you also take colchicine, an NSAID, a diuretic, or a blood thinner. **Get urgent care (or call 911) if** you develop a skin rash with fever, blistering, peeling, mouth or eye sores, swelling of the face or lips, or yellowing of the skin or eyes. These can be signs of a rare but serious allergic reaction to allopurinol.

## How Allopurinol Works (and Why Alcohol Works Against It)

Gout happens when there's too much **uric acid** in your blood. Uric acid is a normal waste product your body makes when it breaks down **purines**, compounds found in your own cells and in many foods and drinks. When levels stay high, uric acid can form needle-shaped crystals in and around joints. Your immune system attacks those crystals, and that's the sudden, intensely painful, hot, swollen joint of a gout flare, often in the big toe.

Allopurinol lowers uric acid by blocking an enzyme called **xanthine oxidase**. That enzyme handles the last steps of turning purines into uric acid. With it partly switched off, your body makes less uric acid. Over months, lower levels let existing crystals slowly dissolve, and flares become less frequent. Allopurinol is a long-term, preventive medicine. It doesn't treat a flare that's already happening.

Alcohol pushes uric acid up through several routes at once:

1. **It makes your body produce more uric acid.** Breaking down alcohol in the liver uses up the cell's energy molecule (ATP) quickly. The breakdown of all that used ATP releases purines, which then get turned into uric acid. So drinking increases the raw material for uric acid, independent of anything you eat.
2. **It makes your kidneys clear less uric acid.** Alcohol metabolism raises lactic acid in the blood. Your kidneys use the same exit route for lactate and urate, so when lactate is high, less uric acid gets flushed out in urine and more stays in your blood.
3. **Some drinks bring their own purines.** Beer is the standout. It contains a purine called guanosine, largely from the brewing yeast, on top of the alcohol itself. That's a big part of why beer behaves worse than other drinks in gout studies.
4. **It dehydrates you.** Alcohol increases urine output for a while, and a night out often means less water and more salty food. Concentrated blood and lower fluid intake make crystal formation more likely.

Allopurinol only addresses part of this picture. It slows how much uric acid you make, but it doesn't stop alcohol from reducing how much your kidneys excrete, and it can be overwhelmed if you keep adding a large purine and alcohol load. That's why doctors describe alcohol as working against gout treatment rather than reacting with the pill.

## Does Alcohol Make Allopurinol Less Effective?

In a practical sense, yes, if you drink regularly or heavily. Not because alcohol changes how the drug is absorbed or broken down, but because it keeps adding to the problem the drug is trying to solve.

Think of uric acid as water in a bathtub. Allopurinol turns the tap down. Alcohol turns the tap back up a bit and partly blocks the drain. With a little alcohol now and then, the tub still drains fine. With steady drinking, the level stays higher than your doctor is aiming for, and you may need a higher dose to reach your target, or you may keep having flares despite treatment.

Most gout specialists aim to keep blood uric acid below **6 mg/dL** (some aim lower for people with tophi). This "treat to target" approach is the core of the American College of Rheumatology's 2020 gout guideline, which also conditionally recommends that people with gout limit alcohol, whatever their stage of disease. If you're on allopurinol and your levels aren't coming down as expected, alcohol is one of the first things your doctor will ask about.

A useful way to check: your blood uric acid test results. If you're drinking and your numbers are on target, your current pattern probably isn't undoing your treatment. If your numbers are stubbornly high, an honest conversation about how much you drink is worth having before your dose keeps climbing.

## Can You Drink Beer on Allopurinol?

Beer is the drink most strongly linked to gout, so it deserves its own answer.

A large study of more than 47,000 male health professionals, published in *The Lancet* in 2004 (Choi and colleagues), followed men over 12 years. Beer showed the strongest association with developing gout, spirits had a smaller association, and moderate wine drinking showed no clear increase in risk. Other research on uric acid levels in the general population has pointed the same way.

What this means if you're on allopurinol:

- **Beer is the drink most likely to undo your treatment.** It brings both alcohol and extra purines.
- **Non-alcoholic beer is not purine-free.** It removes the alcohol, which is the bigger effect, but it can still contain some purines from the yeast and malt. It's generally a much better choice than regular beer, though not something to drink by the six-pack if you're prone to flares. If you're curious about what's actually in it, see our guide on [whether non-alcoholic beer has alcohol](/never-hungover/does-non-alcoholic-beer-have-alcohol).
- **"Light" beer has less alcohol but still has the yeast purines.** It's better than a strong craft ale, not a free pass.
- **Big beer sessions are the riskiest pattern of all.** Several pints in one sitting, plus salty bar food and not much water, is close to a recipe for a flare.

If beer is your drink of choice, the honest advice is to have it rarely and in small amounts, and to switch to something else most of the time.

## Allopurinol and Wine or Spirits

In the 2004 study above, moderate wine drinking (roughly a glass or two a day) wasn't associated with a clear increase in gout risk, while spirits showed a smaller association than beer. Some later work on gout flares, though, found that **any kind of alcohol** raised the short-term risk of an attack when people drank more than usual.

That later research is worth knowing about. A study published in the *American Journal of Medicine* in 2014 (Neogi and colleagues) followed people who already had gout and asked about their drinking in the day or two before each flare. Drinking more than usual in a 24-hour period was linked to a higher chance of a flare, and the risk rose with the number of drinks. Wine, beer, and spirits all showed this effect.

So the takeaway is roughly:

- **For long-term uric acid, beer is worst, spirits are middle, and wine appears least harmful in moderation.**
- **For triggering a flare, the amount you drink in one go matters more than the type.** A heavy night on wine can still set off an attack.
- **Sugary mixers add another problem.** Drinks sweetened with fructose, including regular soda and many cocktail mixers, also raise uric acid. A spirit with soda water or diet mixer is a better choice than a rum and cola.

## How Long After Taking Allopurinol Can You Drink?

There's no special waiting period. Allopurinol is usually taken once a day, it works by keeping uric acid steadily lower over weeks and months, and a drink a few hours before or after your dose doesn't change how the pill itself works.

What matters more:

- **Keep taking your dose every day, including the day you drink and the day after.** Skipping allopurinol because you're drinking, or stopping during a flare, makes uric acid swing up and down, which can make flares more likely. Most doctors advise continuing allopurinol through a flare.
- **Don't double up the next day.** Taking extra allopurinol won't cancel a night of drinking and increases side-effect risk.
- **Take it after food with a glass of water**, as most patient leaflets advise. That helps with the stomach upset some people get.
- **Drink plenty of water throughout the day.** Allopurinol patient information commonly advises drinking enough fluid to keep your urine output up, partly to reduce the risk of kidney stones. That advice matters even more on a day you drink alcohol.

## The First Few Months Are the Riskiest Time

One thing that surprises a lot of people: starting allopurinol can actually make gout flares *more* likely for a while. As uric acid levels drop, crystals that have built up in your joints start to loosen and dissolve, and that shifting can set off attacks. This is a known effect, not a sign the drug isn't working.

To cover this period, doctors usually start at a low dose and raise it slowly, and many prescribe a flare-prevention medicine alongside it for the first several months, most often low-dose **colchicine** or an **NSAID** such as naproxen. Both of those have their own issues with alcohol:

- **NSAIDs and alcohol** both irritate the stomach lining, and together they raise the risk of stomach bleeding. NSAIDs can also strain the kidneys when you're dehydrated. Our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) explains the stomach and kidney risks in more detail.
- **Colchicine** commonly causes stomach upset and diarrhea, and alcohol can make those side effects worse. Colchicine also needs careful dosing in people with kidney or liver problems.

Put simply, the early months of allopurinol are not the time for heavy drinking. You're already more likely to flare, you may be on a second medicine that doesn't mix well with alcohol, and your doctor is trying to find the right dose using your blood test results.

## Does Allopurinol Affect Your Liver, and Does Alcohol Make That Worse?

Allopurinol is generally well tolerated, but it can occasionally affect the liver. Liver problems from allopurinol are uncommon, and when they do happen they're often part of a wider allergic-type reaction rather than a slow, quiet effect. Doctors typically check liver and kidney blood tests when you start the medicine and periodically after that.

Alcohol is processed mainly by the liver, so heavy drinking adds load on the same organ. For most people taking allopurinol who drink lightly, that's not a big concern. For people who drink heavily, have fatty liver disease, or already have abnormal liver tests, it's a good reason to talk with your doctor before drinking at all.

Signs that something may be wrong with your liver include yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes, dark urine, pale stools, pain under the right ribs, unusual tiredness, or loss of appetite. Any of these while taking allopurinol needs a call to your doctor.

## The Rash Warning: The One Thing Not to Ignore

The most important safety point about allopurinol isn't about alcohol at all, but it matters because people sometimes blame a rash on something they drank or ate.

Allopurinol can, rarely, cause serious skin and allergic reactions, including **Stevens-Johnson syndrome**, **toxic epidermal necrolysis**, and a condition called **DRESS** (a drug reaction with fever, rash, and organ involvement). These usually show up in the first few months of treatment. The risk is higher in people with kidney disease, at higher starting doses, and in people who carry a gene variant called **HLA-B\*58:01**, which is more common in people of Han Chinese, Korean, and Thai descent, and in some people of African descent. Some guidelines recommend testing for this gene before starting allopurinol in higher-risk groups.

Allopurinol's prescribing information is clear: **stop taking it at the first sign of a skin rash** and contact your doctor. That applies even if the rash seems mild, and even if you think it was something else, like a drink you don't usually have. Get urgent care for a rash with fever, blistering, peeling skin, sores in the mouth, eyes, or genitals, or swelling of the face.

## Other Side Effects That Overlap With Drinking

Some of allopurinol's more common side effects can feel a lot like the effects of alcohol, which can make it hard to tell what's causing what:

- **Stomach upset, nausea, or diarrhea.** Both allopurinol and alcohol can do this. Taking allopurinol after food helps.
- **Drowsiness.** Allopurinol's label warns that some people feel drowsy and should be careful about driving or operating machinery until they know how it affects them. Alcohol adds to drowsiness, so don't drive after drinking while you're still learning how the medicine affects you (or at all, frankly).
- **Headache.** This is common with a hangover and occasionally reported with allopurinol.

If side effects are getting worse when you drink, that's useful information for your doctor or pharmacist.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Talk to your doctor before drinking, and consider avoiding alcohol, if any of these apply:

- **You have kidney disease.** Your allopurinol dose is often adjusted for kidney function, your kidneys already struggle to clear uric acid, and dehydration from drinking adds stress. Alcohol is also linked to dehydration-related kidney problems, which we cover in our article on [whether alcohol causes kidney stones](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-cause-kidney-stones).
- **You have frequent flares, tophi, or uric acid kidney stones.** Your treatment target is usually stricter, and you have less room for alcohol to push levels up.
- **You take a diuretic ("water pill")** such as hydrochlorothiazide or furosemide. These can raise uric acid on their own, and combined with alcohol and dehydration the effect adds up.
- **You take azathioprine or mercaptopurine.** Allopurinol interacts strongly with these medicines, and the doses must be managed by your doctor. This isn't about alcohol, but it's one of the most important allopurinol interactions to know about.
- **You take a blood thinner like warfarin.** Allopurinol can affect warfarin levels, and alcohol can as well. Your doctor may need to monitor you more closely.
- **You drink heavily or most days.** At that point the issue isn't how to fit drinking around allopurinol. It's that the drinking itself may be keeping your gout active.

## Practical Tips If You Do Drink

If your doctor is comfortable with you drinking a little, these habits help keep your uric acid and flare risk down:

1. **Keep it light and occasional.** A drink or two on some days is very different from several drinks every day, or a big session once a week.
2. **Choose wine or spirits with a sugar-free mixer over beer.** And avoid fructose-sweetened mixers.
3. **Drink a full glass of water with each alcoholic drink**, and more before bed.
4. **Eat a proper meal, but watch the purine-heavy stuff.** Organ meats, some seafood (anchovies, sardines, shellfish), and large portions of red meat add purines. Pairing a big steak and several beers is a common flare setup.
5. **Never skip allopurinol** on drinking days or the day after.
6. **Have a plan for a flare.** Ask your doctor in advance what you should take if a flare starts, so you're not guessing at 3 a.m. with a swollen toe and a hangover.
7. **Watch the pattern.** If your flares tend to follow nights out, that's a strong sign to cut back further.

For a broader look at why drinking triggers attacks, including which drinks are worst and why, see our full guide to [alcohol and gout](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-gout).

## Is a Gout Flare or a Hangover? When to See a Doctor

The morning after drinking, it's easy to blame every ache on a hangover. A gout flare is different: it usually comes on fast, often overnight, in a single joint (very often the big toe, but also the ankle, knee, wrist, or finger). The joint becomes hot, red, swollen, and so tender that even a bedsheet touching it hurts.

**Contact your doctor if:**

- You have a gout flare while on allopurinol, especially if they're happening more often
- You've just started allopurinol and keep having flares
- You notice new stomach pain, persistent diarrhea, or unusual tiredness

**Get urgent care if:**

- A painful, swollen joint comes with **fever or chills**, or you feel generally very unwell. A hot joint with fever can also be an infected joint, which is an emergency.
- You develop **any rash with fever, blisters, peeling skin, or sores in your mouth or eyes**, or swelling of the face or lips
- You notice **yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs**
- You have **severe pain in your side or back** with blood in your urine, which can be a kidney stone

## Where DHM Fits (Honestly)

People with gout who still enjoy an occasional drink sometimes ask whether hangover supplements can help. Here's the honest picture.

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is in animals and lab settings, with limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers uric acid in people, prevents gout flares, or offsets alcohol's effect on allopurinol. It shouldn't change how much you drink or how you take your medicine, and like any supplement, it's worth running past your doctor or pharmacist before adding it alongside a prescription. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known.

If your doctor is fine with it and you want to try DHM for the occasional night out, two commonly chosen options are [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it. The things that actually protect your joints, though, are the ones above: less alcohol, less beer, more water, and taking your allopurinol every day.

## The Bottom Line

- There's no direct dangerous reaction between allopurinol and alcohol, but alcohol raises uric acid and works against the medicine.
- Beer is the worst drink for gout. Spirits are in the middle, and wine looks least harmful in moderation, but a heavy night of any drink can trigger a flare.
- Keep drinking light and occasional, drink water alongside it, and avoid sugary mixers.
- Keep taking allopurinol every day, including the days you drink. Don't skip it or double up.
- Be extra careful in the first few months of treatment and if you have kidney disease.
- Stop allopurinol and call your doctor at the first sign of a rash. Get urgent help for a rash with fever, blistering, or mouth sores.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking allopurinol?**

Many people on allopurinol can drink a little, occasionally, but alcohol raises uric acid and works against the medicine. There is no dangerous direct reaction between the two. Keep drinking light, avoid beer where you can, drink water alongside it, and keep taking your allopurinol every day. Check with your doctor first if you have kidney disease, frequent flares, or take colchicine, an NSAID, or a diuretic.

**Does alcohol make allopurinol less effective?**

Not by changing how the drug is absorbed, but in practice regular or heavy drinking can partly cancel it out. Allopurinol lowers how much uric acid you make, while alcohol increases uric acid production and makes your kidneys clear less of it. People who drink often may need a higher dose to reach their uric acid target or may keep having flares.

**Can I drink beer on allopurinol?**

Beer is the drink most strongly linked to gout because it brings both alcohol and purines from brewing yeast. If you drink it at all, keep it rare and small. Wine or a spirit with a sugar-free mixer is generally a better choice, and non-alcoholic beer is better than regular beer, though not completely purine-free.

**How long after taking allopurinol can I drink alcohol?**

There's no special waiting period. Allopurinol works by keeping uric acid steadily lower over weeks and months, so the timing of a drink relative to your daily dose doesn't change how the pill works. What matters is taking it every day, including the day you drink and the day after, and drinking plenty of water.

**Should I skip allopurinol if I'm going to drink?**

No. Skipping doses makes uric acid levels swing, which can make flares more likely. Take your usual dose, don't double up the next day, and keep drinking light. Most doctors also advise continuing allopurinol during a gout flare unless they tell you otherwise.

**Is wine OK with allopurinol?**

In a large 2004 study published in The Lancet, moderate wine drinking wasn't clearly linked to a higher risk of developing gout, unlike beer and spirits. But later research found that drinking more than usual of any type of alcohol, wine included, raised the short-term risk of a flare. A glass with dinner is very different from a bottle.

**Can alcohol trigger a gout flare even if I'm on allopurinol?**

Yes. Allopurinol lowers the risk of flares over time, but a heavy drinking session can still set one off, especially in the first few months of treatment when flares are more common anyway. If your flares tend to follow nights out, that's a strong sign to cut back and to tell your doctor.

**When should I see a doctor about allopurinol and alcohol?**

Stop allopurinol and call your doctor at the first sign of any skin rash. Get urgent care for a rash with fever, blistering, peeling, or mouth or eye sores, for yellow skin or eyes or dark urine, or for a hot swollen joint with fever. Also see your doctor if you keep having flares on treatment.
